newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Early chaos as Nicaraguans vote.
newsitem.headline: Early chaos as Nicaraguans vote.

text.p: In an election marred by initial confusion and delays, Nicaraguans voted on Sunday for a new president with the main choice between a former Sandinista revolutionary and a right-winger backed by allies of late former dictator Anastasio Somoza.
Voters have to choose from 23 candidates but polls say only two -- right-wing lawyer Arnoldo Aleman and Washington's old bogeyman, Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega -- have any real chance of winning.

Confusion and technical glitches delayed the scheduled start of voting but slowly voters trickled into the 8,995 polling stations to make their choice on the three-foot (one metre) -long ballot paper.
Interviewed after casting their votes at different locations in the capital Managua, Aleman and Ortega both boasted they would win and shrugged off the early hitches.
First results from the 2.4 million voters were expected early on Monday. The winner must poll 45 percent to avoid a second round run-off in late November or early December.
"We're seeing how complicated the voting procedure is. There are six elections going on simultaneously," said former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, monitoring the ballot.
He said confusion among voters and failure to deliver election materials had snagged the start of polling in what he termed the most complex election he has ever witnessed.
During a bitter campaign in Nicaragua, the second poorest country in the Americas after Haiti, the left-right struggle that has torn the nation apart for much of this century was played out again.

Topping voter preferences going into Sunday's poll was Aleman, 50, running for the right-wing Liberal Alliance. His backers include Miami exiles formerly allied to the brutal Somoza family dictatorship which ruled Nicaragua for much of this century -- and which Aleman refuses to condemn.

Just behind him was Ortega, the leader of Nicaragua's revolutionary Sandinistas who overthrew Somoza, fought former U.S. President Ronald Reagan's Contra rebels and governed the country from 1979 to 1990 before losing power in an election to current centrist President Violeta Chamorro.
"We no longer have Somoza, there is no war with Reagan, there is no (economic embargo). Now the fight we have is against poverty," Ortega told reporters after voting.
Analysts say Nicaragua's poor will decide the result.

In a country where more than half the population lacks a proper job, both Aleman and Ortega have pledged economic recovery and strong leadership after the rudderless six-year rule of Chamorro -- Latin America's only female head of state.

"I have to wait here as long as it takes. That horrible man (Ortega) can't win the election after all he has done," said Maria Alicia Cesar, 26, who waited in line to vote for Aleman with her maid at hand and her Toyota Land Cruiser parked nearby.
Ortega supporters call Aleman the candidate of the rich, who did nothing for the poor as mayor of Managua.
"It will be a sad day for the poor if Aleman wins," said Jose Laguna, 39, a street sweeper.
Both Aleman and Ortega have sought to paint themselves as modern, business-friendly moderates with development and reconciliation at the top of their agendas.
The United States -- which earlier said it "would not use the word democrat to describe Daniel Ortega" -- has assured voters it will respect the vote whichever way it goes.
"We're not taking sides in this election. We can accept whoever the Nicaraguan people select," Brian Atwood, President Bill Clinton's envoy to the elections, said late on Saturday.
In rural regions in northern Nicaragua, swollen rivers from days of lashing rain hampered authorities trying to deliver voting materials to far-flung villages, officials said.
In Matagalpa department, one of the main theatres of the Contra rebels' eight-year war against the Sandinistas, army choppers were still flying in voting materials on Sunday morning.
Apart from choosing the president, voters will also choose a vice president, 145 mayors and 145 councillors, 90 federal deputies and 20 members of the Central American parliament.
